sections.html: Parapteronotus bonapartii can reach a total length of up to 40-50 cm. Suggested common name: duckbill knifefish.
Mainly they get live Tubifex, which are taken readily.

Apteronotus species are known to be sometimes quite nasty against each other, so the two fish are kept separated. The animals have very obvious teeth. The purpose of the teeth is unknown so far. The knifefish do not feed on small fish.

Most South American knifefish are only weakly electric and use the electric pulses for orientation and communication.
The snout of the male grows constantly when the individual reaches sexual maturity. The male was once described as a separate species, Apteronotus anas, with a grotesque, enormous snout.

Nothing is known about the breeding behaviour of Parapteronotus bonapartii. However, the close relative Apteronotus leptorhynchus has been bred in aquaria already (Kirschbaum & Schugardt, 2002). The latter species does not take broodcare in any way.

The history of its scientific names is long and complicated. In 1942 Eigenmann and Allen described a knifefish with an enormous snout as Apteronotus anas. In 2002 it was found that A. anas is only the fertile male of Apteronotus hasemani, described in 1913, so the name Apteronotus anas became a synonym (invalid name). One year earlier, Albert (2001) had described the genus Parapteronotus for A. hasemani. In 2007 Triques showed that A. hasemani is identical with the species described in 1855 by Castelnau as Sternarchus bonapartii. The currently valid name is therefore Parapteronotus bonapartii.

Lexicon: Apteronotus: ancient Greek, "with no fin on the back". Parapteronotus: ancient Greek, "close to Apteronotus". leptorhynchus: ancient Greek, "with a small snout". hasemani: dedicated to J. D. Haseman. Sternarchus: ancient Greek, "breastbone-anus". bonapartii: dedicated to prince Charles Bonaparte, "a prince of science". anas: Latin, "duck".
